data.targetWord: According to Maimonides, the Messiah will fulfil specific prophecies: rebuilding the Temple, gathering all Jews to Israel, ushering in an era of universal peace, and bringing all nations to recognise God.
Jews reject the Christian belief that Jesus was the Messiah, because he did not fulfil the key prophecies (rebuilding the Temple, universal peace). For Jews, the Messiah is still awaited.

data.sourceWord: Covenant with Abraham — personal relationship with God

'I will make you into a great nation and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing.' (Genesis 12:2) — the foundational promise of the Abrahamic covenant.

data.targetWord: Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement) is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Jews fast for 25 hours, attend synagogue for extended prayers including Kol Nidre, and seek God's forgiveness for sins of the past year.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — importance of Yom Kippur

data.targetWord: Before Yom Kippur, Jews must seek forgiveness from any person they have wronged — God can only forgive sins against him, not against others. The day culminates in the Neilah service and the blowing of the shofar.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — importance of Yom Kippur

data.targetWord: Rosh Hashanah (Jewish New Year) begins the Ten Days of Awe leading to Yom Kippur. The shofar (ram's horn) is blown as a call to repentance, and Jews eat apples and honey for a sweet new year.

data.sourceWord: Rosh Hashanah contrasted with Yom Kippur
data.targetWord: Rosh Hashanah is a day of celebration and hope for the new year, while Yom Kippur ten days later is solemn and penitential. Together they form the High Holy Days, the most spiritually serious period of the year.
Shabbat (Saturday) is the weekly day of rest commanded in the Torah. Observant Jews light candles, recite Kiddush over wine, attend synagogue, and refrain from the 39 categories of forbidden work.

Shabbat provides a weekly opportunity for prayer, Torah study, family time, and spiritual renewal. It commemorates both God's rest at creation and the Jewish people's liberation from slavery in Egypt.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: Shabbat commanded in the Torah

data.title: The High Holy Days in Judaism
data.sourceTitle: The High Holy Days in Judaism
data.sourcePassage: The High Holy Days (Yamim Nora'im — 'Days of Awe') are the most spiritually significant period in the Jewish calendar. They begin with Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year) and end ten days later with Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement). Rosh Hashanah is a day of celebration and reflection. The shofar (ram's horn) is blown to call the community to repentance. Jews eat apples dipped in honey to symbolise hopes for a sweet new year, and attend synagogue for extended prayers. Jewish tradition teaches that on Rosh Hashanah God opens the Book of Life and begins to judge each person's deeds from the past year. The ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are used for reflection and seeking forgiveness from those one has wronged. Yom Kippur itself is a day of fasting, prayer and confession. Jews spend much of the day in synagogue, reciting confessional prayers and asking God for forgiveness. The day ends with the Neilah (closing) service and a final, long blast of the shofar, after which Jews break their fast.
